items.title: Barney Bigard Interview, Early 1970s
items.q: I marched with, uh, Buddy Petit.

ctx.x: Now you're talking about these marching bands, uh, the bands of New Orleans, you know, going to the funeral and, uh, other occasions and all. Who were some of the people that you might have, uh, marched with? Was Louis Armstrong along with you at the time?

No. I marched with, uh, Buddy Petit. I marched with a guy named Chris Kelly. I marched with, uh, Manuel Perez. Mm-hmm. And, uh, there was a clarinetist, uh, I can't think of his name offhand. Well, he used to play so beautiful at a funeral that all of the women would start crying when they'd start playing. And, uh, but he moved, well, he left New Orleans and he went, and the last time I saw him, that was years ago, he was living in Philadelphia. Mm-hmm. I'll think of his name during the course of the night. But…

Well, now, I know that, uh, today most people have an idea of what the Duke Ellington band sounds like. I mean, the minute you first hear the first few notes, you say, that's Duke Ellington. But I'm sure that when we start playing this next one, that, uh, if we weren't to identify the band, that might take them a bit of a time, unless there are real jazz buffs, to identify this sound. Because this one goes back to, I believe, about 1929, 1930, when Duke Ellington was at the Cotton Club. And we have one called,…

items.title: 68113_Barney Bigard oral history interview
items.q: And I happened to be working with him at that time

ctx.x: You know, in New Orleans they didn't have any union musicians for colored people. So they'd take jobs and get a deposit. And Buddy Petit was very popular at that time, and he'd take all the jobs he could to get the deposit to go and drink.

Well, I was a youngster and I didn't -- I got in on the tail end of his career and the beginning of mine. So they had -- every year the longshoremen, they gave a big picnic in a big lake, a big party with all the different unions. And I happened to be working with him at that time, and we were doing good and playing pretty good. I was scuffling like as usual because I didn't know much about it. So there was a cop stationed on the bandstand. So when we had finished a set, the cop asked some of the guys in the…
Petit?" And one boy would say, "The trumpet man right there. That man." So the cop would say, "Oh, that can't be Buddy Petit." He says, "Don't tell me that can't be Buddy Petit. That's Buddy Petit."
